not_claimed: HCSF initial and renewal fee schedule beyond the $500 application fee and $500 per-location annual fee. N.J.A.C. 13:45B-7.1 and the text of 13:45B-13.5 were not retrieved; the annual fee comes from a law-firm summary.

Official text of P.L. 2026, c.45 and any DCA rule proposals implementing it. Details rely on a Holland & Knight summary. Whether registrations that expired Sept. 30, 2026 can still be renewed, and on what terms, must be confirmed with DCA.

Annual financial statement due date. Rule text says July 1 each year [S5], while the law firm reports a Sept. 30 registration date [S3]; the sources conflict and the current due date is unconfirmed. The audit and enhanced financial reporting rules (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A(b)-(e)) are reported as suspended, with current thresholds unverified.
Penalty for operating unregistered. A $500-per-day figure appears in 2020 legislation, but its enactment was not verified; no penalty amount is claimed.

HCSF staffing ratios, administrator or manager qualifications and training hours, inspection or survey process and frequency, capacity limits, and zoning or siting rules for HCSF offices. None were found in primary text.

Whether the $1,000,000 liability insurance is a registration-document requirement under a specific rule subsection (the DCA FAQ states it; the governing subsection was not confirmed). Workers' compensation manual rate for the home health/personal care class code (only the overall -4.3% rate-level change was found) [S33]. Actual insurance premiums are not claimed.
Current official FFS PCA rate after July 1, 2024. A secondary source mentions a 2026 fee schedule (SPA NJ-26-0002) but no verified rate was found, so $26.68 is the latest verified.

MCO-level PCA and MLTSS personal care contracted rates, 2026 MCO rate changes, and managed-care-plan credentialing or network-openness for new agencies. The Horizon $25.16/hour minimum (effective 7/1/2023) conflicts with the later $26.68 FFS rate and is not treated as the current MCO rate.

PPP wage schedule. A secondary source says no public PPP rate card exists; the state only says the budget is authorized hours × the current rate. Fiscal intermediary assignments by MCO come only from secondary sources.
Text of N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8 on the 40-hour weekly PCA cap and the family-member exception; the cap comes from secondary guides only.

CY2026 Medicaid provider enrollment steps and fees (NJMMIS/DMAHS). A secondary source cites a $730 application fee, which is not verified, and current MLTSS/PCA provider enrollment requirements were not retrieved from DMAHS provider pages.
Whether EVV vendor, aggregator or other fees apply to providers. The EVV compliance dates (PCS 1/1/2021; home health 1/1/2023) come from a plan bulletin, not the state.

Number of registered HCSFs, CHHA-employing agencies, or HCSFs accepting Medicaid (an undated industry estimate of fewer than 400 of about 1,000 is not relied on); named competitors; provider market shares; referral volumes.

Number of PCA, PPP or MLTSS participants receiving personal care; current MLTSS enrollment by program; current JACC and PPP waitlist status by county; current AL/AFC slot count and waitlist. Only undated secondary statements exist.

MLTSS waitlist status. The official MLTSS page does not state one; secondary sources conflict on whether MLTSS is a no-cap entitlement or depends on available funds, and on whether NJ still has HCBS waivers.
The NJ 65+ population, I/DD population served, and referral-source data. They were not gathered from official Census or DDD sources.
Local minimum wages in NJ metros (Newark, Jersey City, Paterson, Trenton). Wages must be checked against any local ordinance; none was retrieved.

NJ-specific BLS OEWS May 2025 medians for nursing assistants, administrators (medical and health services managers) and office staff were not retrieved. NJ RN and LPN medians come from secondary summaries that conflict ($106,500 vs $110,100 for RNs) and are not used.
New-employer UI rate and wage base for July 1, 2026–June 30, 2027. Only the July 2025–June 2026 new-employer UI rate (2.6825% UI plus 0.1175% WF/SWF) and the 2026 wage base ($44,800) were verified.

NJ LLC formation fee ($100 vs older $125), annual report fee ($75) and late fee ($25). They come from secondary sources only; franchise/corporation business tax obligations for an NJ LLC were not retrieved.
Commercial office rent benchmarks for NJ metros. HUD FY2026 fair market rents were not used because they measure residential rent, not office space.
Board of Nursing CHHA training-program approval fee, and the current $50 application and $30 biennial renewal fees (the $30 comes from an undated Board form). Confirm on current Board pages.

Effective date of the federal Medicaid changes. DMAHS pages conflict (Fall 2026 vs. Jan. 1, 2027 for work requirements). NJ DHS says more than 540,000 expansion adults would be subject; the impact on personal care demand is not quantified.
Scope note: many quotes came from search-result excerpts of the cited pages, so wording and figures should be re-checked against the live pages before publication.

ACA large-employer cost (IRC §4980H) for the nj_medicaid100 and nj_medicaid200 configurations, which exceed 50 FTEs. Not modeled and amounts not verified; the flat 4% benefits load likely understates cost.

NJ entity-level tax minimums (CBT minimum tax or partnership filing fee per member) and local licence fees. The $0 opex line is a placeholder, so modeled profit is overstated until a CPA supplies the amounts.

Whether the $500 initial application fee covers the first registration year, or whether the $500/year registration fee is additional from month 1 (possible year-1 double-count). Confirm with DCA. Also, the current post-7/1/2024 MCO mandated minimum PCA rate was not found; the $25.16/hour Horizon figure is historical only.

payroll_burden.notes: Payroll tax is the sum of four parts. (1) Employer FICA of 7.65% is the federal statutory rate. (2) The NJ new-employer UI plus WF/SWF rate is 2.80% (2.6825% + 0.1175%) on a $44,800 wage base [S32]. That rate covers July 2025–June 2026; the July 2026–June 2027 rate was not verified. (3) The NJ employer disability rate is 0.50% [S32]. (4) FUTA is about 0.6%, an operator estimate. Workers' compensation is mandatory from the first employee [S41]. The 7% load is an operator estimate, because the class-code manual rate for home care was not retrieved; only an overall 4.3% rate-level decrease effective 1/1/2026 was found [S33]. Benefits at 4% (including paid sick leave) are an operator estimate. The nj_medicaid100 and nj_medicaid200 configurations employ roughly 69 and 139 FTEs (derived, ACA 120-hours-per-month basis), above the 50-FTE federal employer shared-responsibility threshold (IRC §4980H). sections.executive_summary:
New Jersey does not issue a stand-alone 'home care license'. A business that places or arranges personnel to give health care, companion care or personal care in the home of a disabled person or someone 60 or older must register as a **Health Care Service Firm (HCSF)** with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs (DCA) [S1][S3]. The rules sit in N.J.S.A. 34:8-45.1 and N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13 and 13:45B-14 [S2][S3]. Aides placed by the firm must be actively certified Homemaker-Home Health Aides (CHHAs) who are employed by the agency [S6]. The firm must name an NJ-licensed RN or physician as its health care practitioner supervisor [S1]. It must also obtain accreditation from a Department of Human Services-recognized body within 12 months of registration [S25][S26][S3].

Up-front licensing cost is modest. It consists of a **$500 application fee** [S1], a **$10,000 surety bond** (waivable at a net worth of $100,000 or more) [S4], a **$1,000,000 general professional liability certificate** [S1], and a **$500 annual registration fee per primary location** [S3]. DCA reports average processing of 30 to 60 days. That is an average, not a rule deadline [S3]. The larger costs are accreditation, RN oversight, insurance and ramp-up payroll. Registration timing is in flux. P.L. 2026, c.45 (signed July 22, 2026) moved the annual expiration from June 30 to September 30, and DCA guidance on implementation is still pending [S3].

Money comes from two very different streams:

- **Private pay.** CareScout's 2025 survey puts the New Jersey median for non-medical in-home caregivers at **$38 per hour** ($86,944 a year at 44 hours a week), against a national median of $35 [S28][S29].
- **NJ FamilyCare Medicaid.** The state-plan rate for personal care assistant (PCA) services, code T1019, is **$26.68 per hour** (effective July 1, 2024) [S18]. MLTSS members get personal care through managed care plans, and those contracted rates are not public [S16][S17]. One plan's 2023 notice quoted a $25.16 per hour minimum [S20].

The math favors private pay. In the model, a **40-client private-pay agency** nets about **$15,692 a month (14.3% margin)** at 90% census. It breaks even at about 54.6% occupancy and first turns profitable in month 9, with about $116,006 of modeled cash needed. A 60-client private-pay agency nets $23,149 a month (14.1%). A 20-client owner-run agency nets $4,340 (7.9%). Medicaid-only models **lose money** at the verified FFS rate: -$11,307 a month at 100 clients and -$11,037 at 200 clients. A 50/50 mixed 60-client agency is about break-even (-$71 a month). The recommended path is to launch private pay first and add Medicaid volume only once the office and RN supervision are paid for (Sections 8 and 10).
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** HCSFs serve people in their own residences. The statutory definition covers an agency that places or arranges the placement of personnel to provide health care, companion care or personal care for a disabled person or a person age 60 or older [S1]. Typical clients are frail older adults needing help with bathing, dressing, toileting, meals and mobility. Others are adults with disabilities and Medicaid members authorized for personal care. Medicaid-funded PCA services are non-emergent, health-related tasks delivered under NJ FamilyCare [S13]. Medicaid will not authorize PCA when the purpose is companionship, respite or stand-alone supervision [S15]. Private-pay clients can buy those services.

**The agency model.** The firm employs aides, schedules them into client homes and supervises them through a health care practitioner supervisor, who must be an NJ-licensed RN or physician [S1]. The supervisor must document in the patient's record every task delegated to a homemaker-home health aide [S6]. A firm may place only actively certified CHHAs employed by the agency, and a CHHA may not work privately [S6][S7]. Whether non-certified staff may be placed for purely companion tasks was not verified. The financial model assumes all caregivers are agency-employed CHHAs paid the New Jersey home health aide median.

**Regulators.** DCA's Regulated Business Section registers and regulates HCSFs [S7]. The Board of Nursing certifies CHHAs and approves training programs [S7][S8]. The Department of Human Services, Division of Medical Assistance and Health Services (DMAHS), runs NJ FamilyCare, PCA, the Personal Preference Program (PPP) and MLTSS [S13][S16].

**Two businesses in one.** Agencies serve private-pay clients, Medicaid clients, or both, and the economics differ sharply (Sections 4 and 8). If the firm charges individuals a placement fee, it must also hold an employment agency license [S2].
sections.licensing_pathway:
**Step 1 — Form the entity.** Form an NJ LLC or corporation. A secondary source puts the LLC certificate of formation at $100 (an older source lists $125) and the annual report at $75, with a $25 late fee [S42][S43]. Confirm both with the Division of Revenue and Enterprise Services. NJ business tax obligations for the entity were not retrieved.

**Step 2 — Line up the registration package.** Under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.3 each HCSF registers on forms provided by the Director [S4]. The package includes:

- a registration form naming the firm, locations, officers, 10%-or-greater owners and managing agents [S4];
- a **$10,000 bond** to secure compliance with the Act. The Director may waive it for a corporation or entity with a net worth of $100,000 or more [S4];
- a signed certification from each officer, director, principal or owner stating whether he or she has ever been convicted of a crime [S4];
- a list of any health licenses held in other states and any actions taken [S4];
- designation of a **health care practitioner supervisor** (NJ-licensed RN or physician) and a copy of the license [S1];
- a **certificate of general professional liability insurance of $1,000,000** [S1].

**Step 3 — File online and pay the fee.** Applications are filed through the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal [S3]. The **$500 application fee** is part of the online initial application [S1].

**Step 4 — Wait for approval.** DCA reports processing on average within 30 to 60 days [S3]. This is a reported average, not a rule-stated deadline. Do not admit clients or place aides before registration is issued.

**Step 5 — Obtain accreditation.** The firm must obtain accreditation from a Department of Human Services-recognized accrediting body within 12 months of registration [S25][S26][S3]. Renewal requires evidence of accreditation (in effect from May 21, 2019) [S27]. Any loss of accreditation must be reported to DCA within 10 days [S3].

**Step 6 — Maintain and renew.**

- The annual registration fee is $500 per primary location (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-7.1 as cited by the law-firm source) [S3].
- Changes to application information must be reported in writing within 30 calendar days [S4].
- P.L. 2026, c.45 moved the annual expiration from June 30 to September 30. Registrations that already renewed for 2026-2027 are automatically extended to September 30, 2027 [S3]. Because September 30, 2026 has already passed, a new applicant must confirm with DCA the registration term and renewal date that will apply.
- Rule text requires an annual financial statement by July 1 [S5]. The law firm reports the audit and enhanced financial reporting provisions (N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A(b)-(e)) as suspended, but says the annual statement is still required [S3]. The sources conflict on dates, so confirm the current due date with DCA.

**Step 7 — Medicaid enrollment (optional).** Medicaid PCA billing requires provider enrollment and managed care credentialing, plus EVV. CY2026 enrollment steps and fees were not retrieved (see not_claimed).

**Not found:** no administrator qualifications, staffing ratios, capacity limits, zoning rules or inspection schedule for HCSFs were located in primary text.
sections.reimbursement:
**Private pay.** Most agencies start here. CareScout's 2025 survey (fielded July to November 2025, released March 2026) puts the New Jersey median for non-medical in-home caregivers at $38 per hour, or $86,944 a year at 44 hours a week. The national median is $35 per hour [S28][S29]. Genworth's 2024 survey published New Jersey monthly figures of $6,864 for homemaker services and $7,055 for a home health aide [S30]. The CareScout figure is a statewide median for non-medical in-home care, not an agency-specific price, so check local competitors, especially in higher-cost metros.

**NJ FamilyCare PCA (fee-for-service).** The State Plan sets the PCA rate for weekday and weekend services at **$26.68 per hour**, effective July 1, 2024 (SPA 24-0013) [S18]. It replaced $23.00 per hour effective January 1, 2022 [S19]. PCA is billed under **T1019 in 15-minute units** for MCOs and FFS [S21], which is $6.67 per unit (derived: $26.68 ÷ 4). A 2026 fee schedule was not verified.

**MLTSS and managed care.** MLTSS operates under the NJ FamilyCare Comprehensive Demonstration Waiver. NJ FamilyCare managed care organizations coordinate all MLTSS services [S16]. Personal care is a covered MLTSS service alongside respite and the personal emergency response system [S17]. In practice an agency is paid by the member's managed care plan, not directly by the state for each service. MCO-contracted PCA rates are **not public**. Horizon NJ Health's 2023 notice states a state-mandated minimum of $6.29 per 15-minute unit ($25.16 per hour) effective July 1, 2023 [S20]. That is below the later FFS rate, and it is one plan's historical notice. The model uses the $26.68 FFS rate as a benchmark assumption, which may overstate MCO revenue.

**Rules that limit Medicaid revenue.**

- Need for PCA must be certified in writing by a physician or practitioner at application and annually [S14].
- PCA is not authorized when the purpose is companionship, respite or stand-alone supervision [S15].
- Secondary guides report a cap of 40 hours per calendar work week under N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(g). The code text was not retrieved [S15].
- EVV is mandatory for Medicaid personal care [S24]. A plan bulletin reports personal care services have been required to use EVV since January 1, 2021 [S47].

**Self-directed PCA.** Self-directed PCA is paid under a 1915(j) reimbursement methodology [S22], and the Personal Preference Program (PPP) is DMAHS's self-directed model [S13]. The state publishes no PPP wage schedule. Participants hire their own aides, so agencies should not assume PPP is an agency revenue source.

**Eligibility context.** MLTSS clinical eligibility for adults 21 and older requires hands-on help with three or more ADLs, or supervision and cueing if cognitively impaired [S16]. A secondary source gives the 2026 single-applicant limits as $2,982 per month income and $2,000 in assets [S40].

**Payment timing.** Medicaid payment lag and EVV claim-denial rates were not verified. The model's working-capital figure reflects ramp-up payroll only.
sections.demand:
**Medicaid population.** As of June 2026, NJ FamilyCare enrolled **1,799,053** people. The Aged, Blind and Disabled (ABD) group totaled **305,168**, including **107,921** in the Aged category and **196,382** in the Disabled category (the category counts are as published, and the two do not sum to the ABD total) [S39]. The state reported **65,102** individuals in home and community-based waiver programs [S39]. Essex County alone had 37,894 ABD members, 11,087 of them aged [S39]. These are eligibility counts, not counts of people receiving personal care. No official count of PCA, PPP or MLTSS personal care recipients was found.

**How Medicaid clients find agencies.** Adults 21 and older seeking MLTSS are directed to the county Area Agency on Aging / Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) for screening [S16]. Once enrolled, members receive services through a managed care plan, so referrals flow through plan care managers and member choice. Which plans' networks are open to new agencies was not verified.

**Private-pay demand.** The CareScout survey shows New Jersey at $38 per hour versus a $35 national median [S28][S29]. High prices show families are paying, but they also mean private clients are price-sensitive and compare agencies. Typical private referral sources are hospital discharge planners, senior living communities, elder-law attorneys and online search. This is an inference, and no New Jersey referral-volume data was found.

**Pending headwinds and tailwinds.**

- DMAHS says federal changes begin in Fall 2026 [S45], while its work-requirements page says certain adults 19 to 64 on NJ FamilyCare Plan ABP must meet requirements beginning January 1, 2027 [S44]. Most affected members must renew every 6 months instead of 12 [S45].
- NJ DHS says more than 540,000 expansion adults would be subject to community engagement requirements [S46].
- These rules mainly target expansion adults, not the older and disabled members who use personal care, so the effect on personal care demand is not quantified.

**Not found:** the number of registered HCSFs, the share accepting Medicaid, MLTSS or JACC/PPP waitlist status, the NJ 65+ population, and competitor names or market shares.
sections.operations:
**Staffing rules that are documented.**

- Only actively certified CHHAs employed by the agency may be placed [S6]. A CHHA may not work privately [S7].
- CHHA certification requires completing a Board-approved training program of at least 76 hours (60 classroom plus 16 clinical) [S8].
- The Board will not certify an aide until a criminal history check clears [S8].
- The aide application fee is $50, and the biennial renewal fee is cited at $30 on an undated Board form [S10][S11]. Certificates renew every two years [S9].
- The health care practitioner supervisor (NJ-licensed RN or physician) must be designated at registration [S1] and must document every delegated task in the patient's record [S6].
- Medicaid PCA clients need written certification of need by a physician or practitioner at application and annually [S14].

**Not documented in the sources:** the supervisor's hours or caseload, aide-to-client ratios, administrator qualifications and training hours, and inspection frequency. The model's RN hours (0.25 FTE at 20 clients, 0.5 FTE at 40, 1 FTE at 60) are operator estimates. Confirm what DCA and your accreditor expect.

**Required systems.**

- **Scheduling and billing software** with an EVV interface. EVV is mandatory for Medicaid personal care [S24]. NJ EVV tools include mobile apps, landline phones and FOB devices [S24]. HHAeXchange hosts NJ's EVV specification, with T1019 billed in 15-minute units [S21]. Whether providers pay EVV or aggregator fees was not found.
- **Accreditation** with a DHS-recognized body, started early and maintained, with loss reported to DCA within 10 days [S25][S3].
- **Insurance:** a $1,000,000 general professional liability certificate at registration [S1]. Workers' compensation is required from the first employee, and going uninsured exposes an employer to fines and a possible stop-work order [S41]. Premiums are operator estimates.
- **Change reporting:** written notice of changes to application information within 30 calendar days [S4].

**Payroll.** The model burden is 22.55% of wages. It includes federal FICA of 7.65%, NJ new-employer UI plus WF/SWF of 2.80% on a $44,800 wage base, employer disability of 0.50% [S32], about 0.6% FUTA (operator estimate), 7% workers' comp (operator estimate; the class rate was not retrieved) [S33] and 4% benefits (operator estimate). The UI rate quoted covers July 2025 to June 2026, and the 2026-2027 rate was not verified.
sections.market_conditions:
**Pricing.** New Jersey's private-pay median of $38 per hour is above the $35 national median [S28][S29]. Genworth's 2024 survey showed $6,864 per month for homemaker services and $7,055 for a home health aide [S30], so private prices keep rising. Medicaid pays much less. The FFS rate of $26.68 is about 30% below $38 (derived), and the 2023 Horizon minimum of $25.16 is lower still [S18][S20].

**Wages.** The NJ median for home health and personal care aides is **$37,090 a year (about $17.83 an hour)**. The 25th percentile is $34,680 (about $16.67) and the 75th is $44,580 (about $21.43) [S34]. The US median for this occupation is $35,800 [S35]. Nationally, nursing assistants earn a median of $42,260, or $38,040 in home healthcare services [S36], so aides can leave for facility jobs. The NJ statewide minimum wage is $15.92 for most employers and $15.23 for employers with fewer than 6 employees under the small-employer schedule [S31]. All modeled aide wages exceed the minimum. Higher local minimum wages in NJ cities were not retrieved. For nurses, the national RN median is $97,550 and the LPN median is $64,400 [S37][S38]. The model uses the national RN median for the supervisor, and the NJ RN wage is probably higher.

**Supply.** An undated industry guide estimated fewer than 400 of roughly 1,000 licensed HCSFs accept Medicaid. This is unofficial and not relied on. No official provider count was retrieved.

**Regulatory churn.** P.L. 2026, c.45 changed the registration calendar, and DCA has suspended the enhanced financial reporting rules while it updates regulations [S3]. Expect further rule changes. Accreditation is now a standing requirement [S25][S27].

**Medicaid policy.** Federal changes to Medicaid and work requirements are coming, but the dates conflict between DMAHS pages (Fall 2026 versus January 1, 2027) [S44][S45]. A secondary source says access to ABD long-term care benefits depends on available funds [S40], and that source conflicts with others on waitlists. This is not resolved.
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the P&L is built.** Revenue per client per month is rate × hours × payer share. Aide hours scale with census at 83.2 hours per client-month, which is 80 billable hours plus 4% paid non-billable time. Both figures are operator estimates, not sourced productivity data. Aides are paid the NJ median of $17.83 an hour [S34], plus a 22.55% payroll burden. Fixed costs are the administrator, RN supervisor, coordinators, office lease and licensing, insurance, accreditation and software. Rent is fixed and sized to each configuration. Occupancy defaults to 90% (80% conservative, 100% optimistic), which is an operator assumption.

**Results at 90% occupancy.**

| Configuration | Net / month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Modeled cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Private pay, 20 clients | $4,340 | 7.9% | 70.4% | 8 | $69,020 |
| **Private pay, 40 clients (default)** | **$15,692** | **14.3%** | **54.6%** | **9** | **$116,006** |
| Private pay, 60 clients | $23,149 | 14.1% | 55.2% | 10 | $188,309 |
| Mixed 60 (50% private / 50% Medicaid PCA) | -$71 | -0.1% | 90.2% | not reached | $296,695 |
| Medicaid PCA, 100 clients | -$11,307 | -5.9% | 135.5% | not reached | $627,408 |
| Medicaid PCA, 200 clients | -$11,037 | -2.9% | 112.2% | not reached | $895,980 |

Break-even occupancy above 100% means the configuration cannot break even even when full under the stated assumptions.

**Why private pay works.** At $38 per hour and 80 hours, a client brings in $3,040 a month. Aide cost with burden is about $1,818 (derived: $17.83 × 83.2 × 1.2255). After per-client costs the contribution is roughly $1,100 per client (derived). At 36 active clients, that covers the fixed team and leaves $15,692 a month.

**Why Medicaid does not work on these assumptions.** At $26.68 and 80 hours, revenue is $2,134 per client. The same aide cost leaves only about $250 per client after per-client costs (derived). That cannot cover an RN, an administrator, EVV and billing coordinators and an office. Scale alone does not fix it. The 200-client agency still loses $11,037 a month.

**Rate at which Medicaid breaks even (derived approximations, all other assumptions unchanged).**

- 100-client Medicaid agency: about **$28.25 per hour** (that is, +$1.57 on $26.68).
- 200-client Medicaid agency: about **$27.45 per hour**.
- Mixed 60 agency: about **$26.71 per hour** on the Medicaid half, effectively break-even at $26.68.

MCO rates are not public. If an MCO pays the 2023 Horizon minimum of $25.16 [S20], these results worsen by about $1.50 an hour, which is roughly $8,600 a month for a 100-client agency at 90% census (derived).

**Sensitivities on the default 40-client private-pay agency (derived estimates).**

- **Price at the national median of $35 instead of $38 [S29]:** net falls to about $7,200 a month. Break-even price is about $32.50 per hour.
- **Hours of 60 per client-month instead of 80:** net falls to about $5,100 a month.
- **Aides at the NJ 75th percentile ($21.43) [S34]:** net falls to about $2,500 a month.
- **Aides at the NJ 25th percentile ($16.67) [S34]:** net rises about $4,300 a month. This carries recruiting risk.
- **Occupancy:** the agency breaks even at 54.6%. At the 80% conservative occupancy it is still profitable, but at lower margin.

**A Medicaid path with lower wages.** If a 200-client Medicaid agency pays the 25th-percentile wage, it would move to roughly +$10,000 a month (derived), and the 100-client agency would be near break-even. That depends on recruiting at $16.67, on MCO rates holding at least at $26.68 and on 80 hours per client being achievable under the authorization process. None of these is verified.

**Wage caveat.** Local minimum wages in NJ cities were not retrieved. All modeled aide wages are above the $15.92 state minimum [S31], so a higher local minimum would only matter if it exceeded $17.83. Re-check in your own city.

**Assumptions to treat as unverified.** Office rent (about $1,200 to $5,500 a month by size), insurance premiums, accreditation costs, supervisor hours, coordinator staffing, administrator salaries and the 90% occupancy are operator estimates. HUD residential rents were deliberately not used as an office rent proxy. The $0 line for other NJ entity-level taxes is a placeholder, so have a CPA confirm and add any amount. The bond premium and accreditation costs are estimates, and if the net-worth waiver applies, the bond premium goes away.
sections.risks:
**Rate risk.** MCO-contracted PCA rates are not public [S20]. The only MCO figure found ($25.16 per hour, 2023) is below the FFS rate [S18][S20]. On the model's assumptions, Medicaid-heavy agencies lose money even at the FFS rate (Section 8). Do not sign an MCO contract without a rate sheet.

**Regulatory change.** P.L. 2026, c.45 changed the registration calendar. Its text was not retrieved, and DCA implementation guidance is pending [S3]. The audit and enhanced reporting rules are suspended, but the annual financial statement is still required, and the sources conflict on the due date [S3][S5]. Registrations that expired September 30, 2026 may need special handling, so confirm with DCA before filing.

**Accreditation.** A DHS-recognized accreditor must accredit you within 12 months of registration, and renewals require evidence of accreditation [S25][S27]. Loss of accreditation must be reported within 10 days [S3]. Failure puts registration at risk. Accreditor fees were not retrieved.

**Workforce.** Only actively certified, agency-employed CHHAs may be placed [S6]. Aides need a 76-hour program and a criminal history check [S8], and certificates renew every two years [S9]. Nursing assistant jobs in other settings pay more (national median $42,260) [S36]. Aide turnover directly affects revenue because hours scale with staff availability.

**Compliance exposure.** Workers' compensation is required from the first employee, and going uninsured can bring fines and a stop-work order [S41]. The HCSF bond and $1,000,000 liability certificate are registration requirements [S1][S4]. Medicaid claims require EVV [S24]. Any penalty for operating unregistered was not verified, so do not operate before registration.

**Medicaid policy.** Federal Medicaid changes and 6-month renewals may reduce coverage continuity for some members [S44][S45], and the timing conflicts across DMAHS pages. The impact on older and disabled personal care recipients is not quantified. Secondary sources conflict on whether access to long-term care benefits depends on funds or has no waitlist [S40].

**Market and price risk.** The $38 benchmark is a statewide median [S28]. A new agency in a competitive metro may have to price lower. At the $35 national median, the default configuration's net falls to about $7,200 a month (Section 8).

**Data gaps.** Administrator qualifications, staffing ratios, inspection process and zoning for HCSFs were not found. Confirm each directly with DCA, your accreditor and the municipality.
sections.recommendations:
**1. Launch private pay first.** The 40-client private-pay agency is the best-supported configuration. It nets $15,692 a month (14.3%), breaks even at 54.6% occupancy and first turns profitable in month 9, with about $116,006 of modeled cash needed. If capital is short, the 20-client owner-administrator model nets $4,340 a month (7.9%) and needs about $69,020, but its break-even is 70.4%, so it has little cushion. The 60-client model nets $23,149 a month (14.1%) with about $188,309 of modeled cash needed. Grow into 60 clients only after referral sources are proven.

**2. Price from local evidence.** Start from the CareScout New Jersey median of $38 per hour [S28]. Check competitor prices in your county. The model's break-even price is about $32.50 per hour on the default configuration, so keep a clear margin above that.

**3. Treat Medicaid as a later add-on.** Wait until the office, RN supervisor and accreditation are paid for. A 60-client mixed agency is roughly break-even (-$71 a month) and needs about $296,695 of modeled cash. Pure Medicaid agencies lose money on the verified rate, and the modeled cash needed is $627,408 at 100 clients and $895,980 at 200 clients. Before entering Medicaid, get written rate sheets from each MCO you would contract with. Only proceed if the T1019 rate gives enough margin. On these assumptions that means at least about $28 to $28.25 per hour, or lower aide wages and fully utilized 80-hour authorizations. Confirm CY2026 provider enrollment fees and steps with DMAHS.

**4. Sequence licensing correctly.**

- Form the entity and line up the bond (or document net worth of $100,000) and the $1,000,000 liability certificate [S1][S4].
- Recruit your NJ-licensed RN or physician supervisor before filing [S1].
- File through the licensure portal with the $500 application fee [S1][S3].
- Call DCA on registration term and renewal timing under P.L. 2026, c.45, and on how the annual financial statement is scheduled [S3][S5].
- Choose a DHS-recognized accreditor and start the process immediately after registration, well inside the 12-month deadline [S25][S26].

**5. Build the team around rules.** Hire only actively certified, agency-employed CHHAs [S6]. Pay at or above the NJ median ($17.83) unless local data shows otherwise [S34]. Keep delegation records complete [S6]. Confirm higher local minimum wages in your city.

**6. Invest in systems early.** Select scheduling, billing and EVV software before launch if you plan to serve Medicaid [S24]. Get quotes for liability, workers' compensation, accreditation and bonding rather than using the model's estimates.

**7. Keep a reserve.** Plan for the modeled cash need, not the licensing fees alone. Ramp-up payroll and Medicaid claim timing drive cash risk.

**8. Re-verify before publishing or acting.** Several quotes came from search-result excerpts and secondary summaries (see not_claimed). Confirm DCA contacts, fee amounts, dates and rule text with the live pages.

checklist.task: Confirm you need a Health Care Service Firm (HCSF) registration
checklist.instructions: An HCSF is an agency that places or arranges for the placement of personnel to provide health care, companion care or personal care services. Under the DCA definition this covers services in the residence of a disabled person or a person aged 60+. If your caregivers will be sent into client homes for hands-on or companion care, plan to register. Confirm scope with the DCA Regulated Business Section before spending money. Cost: $0. Time: 1 day.

checklist.task: Understand that DCA, not the Department of Health, regulates the HCSF
checklist.instructions: The Division of Consumer Affairs Regulated Business Section regulates HCSFs. The Board of Nursing separately certifies the aides. Ignore guides that say the Department of Health issues the HCSF licence. Bookmark the DCA HCSF pages and the Board of Nursing aide pages. Cost: $0. Time: 1 hour.

checklist.task: Choose the business model and payer mix before you form the entity
checklist.instructions: Model results at the 90% default occupancy: a 40-client private-pay agency nets about $15,692/month (14.3% margin), breaks even near 54.6% occupancy and first shows a profit in month 9. A 20-client owner-run agency nets about $4,340/month (7.9%). A 60-client private-pay agency nets about $23,149/month (14.1%). The 60-client mixed agency (50% Medicaid FFS PCA rate) is roughly break-even (-$71/month, 90.2% break-even occupancy). The 100-client and 200-client Medicaid-only models lose money at the $26.68/hour state-plan rate. Start private pay and add Medicaid only after you have verified your MCO contracted rates.
checklist.cite: Pro forma configurations nj_private20/40/60, nj_mixed60, nj_medicaid100/200

checklist.task: Form a New Jersey legal entity (LLC or corporation)
checklist.instructions: File a certificate of formation with the NJ Division of Revenue and Enterprise Services. A secondary source lists the LLC fee at $100 (an older source says $125). Confirm the current fee on the state site. Name the entity so it can be listed accurately on the HCSF registration form. Time: a few days.

checklist.task: Obtain a federal EIN
checklist.instructions: Apply free at irs.gov. It is issued immediately online. You need it for payroll, banking, insurance, the surety bond and any Medicaid enrollment.

checklist.task: Open a business bank account and set up bookkeeping
checklist.instructions: Keep agency funds separate. Your CPA will need clean records for the annual HCSF financial statement and for any net-worth bond waiver (certified financial report). Cost: $0–$30/month for banking. Bookkeeping is modeled at about $600–$800/month with payroll service and legal (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Have a CPA confirm NJ entity-level taxes and fees
checklist.instructions: Franchise or corporation business tax obligations for an NJ LLC, local business licences and any minimum taxes were not verified in this research. The model carries $0 as a placeholder. Ask a CPA to confirm the amounts and add them to the pro forma. Time: 1 consultation.

checklist.task: Calendar the NJ LLC annual report
checklist.instructions: Secondary sources list a $75 annual report fee with a $25 late fee. The deadline is by anniversary month. Confirm on the state site. Budget about $6.25/month.

checklist.task: Decide whether you will charge placement fees to individuals
checklist.instructions: If an HCSF charges individuals a placement fee, it must also hold an employment agency licence. A standard agency model (the client pays the agency for care, and the agency employs the aides) avoids this. Confirm your fee structure in writing with an attorney. Cost: part of attorney review.

checklist.task: Engage a healthcare/employment attorney
checklist.instructions: Have the attorney review your structure, service agreements, employment documents and any Medicaid or MCO contract. Budget $1,500–$5,000 (operator estimate). Ask specifically about the P.L. 2026, c.45 changes and the Sept. 30 registration date.

checklist.task: Line up an NJ-licensed RN or physician as health care practitioner supervisor
checklist.instructions: Registration requires you to designate a health care practitioner supervisor (an NJ-licensed registered professional nurse or physician) and submit a copy of their licence. Verify the licence status on the Board of Nursing lookup. The model assumes an RN at $46.90/hour (national BLS median; NJ is probably higher) at 0.25 FTE for 20 clients, 0.5 FTE for 40 clients and 1 FTE for 60 clients. Those hours are operator estimates; no rule sets supervisor hours.

checklist.task: Obtain the $10,000 surety bond (or qualify for the waiver)
checklist.instructions: Initial registration requires a $10,000 bond to secure compliance with the Act. The Director may waive it for a corporation or entity with a net worth of $100,000 or more. To get a waiver, submit proof such as a certified financial report from a CPA. Otherwise buy the bond from a surety. The premium is an operator estimate of about $100–$500 a year. Get quotes and confirm the premium for your credit profile.

checklist.task: Buy general professional liability insurance of at least $1,000,000
checklist.instructions: The DCA FAQ lists a certificate of general professional liability insurance of $1,000,000 among registration documents. The governing rule subsection was not confirmed. Also quote hired and non-owned auto. Premiums are operator estimates ($400–$700/month in the model). Get at least three broker quotes and ask for the certificate before you file.

checklist.task: Prepare ownership and management disclosures for the registration form
checklist.instructions: The registration form must list firm names, locations, officers, owners of 10% or more and managing agents. Gather legal names, addresses and roles for every person. Time: 1–2 days.

checklist.task: Collect a signed criminal-history certification from each officer, director, principal and owner
checklist.instructions: Each person must certify whether he or she has ever been convicted of a crime. Disclose truthfully. If you have a record, ask counsel before you file. Time: same day per person.

checklist.task: List health licences held in other states, and any actions taken
checklist.instructions: The application requires a list of any licences held in another state by the firm (or its principals), plus any actions taken. Prepare a statement even if the answer is none.

checklist.task: Obtain the other documents the DCA FAQ lists with the online application
checklist.instructions: Read the DCA FAQ's initial-application list line by line and assemble every item (application fee, practitioner supervisor designation, GPL certificate, bond or waiver proof). Items differ from the rule text in places, and the FAQ page was verified from search excerpts only. Re-read the live PDF before filing.

checklist.task: Select a DHS-recognized accrediting body now
checklist.instructions: You must obtain accreditation from a New Jersey Department of Human Services-recognized accrediting body within 12 months of registration. The NJ DHS recognised-body list and accreditor fees were not retrieved. Contact the DHS-recognised bodies for quotes. The model assumes about $150/month amortised (about $5,400 over three years) and a $3,000–$10,000 startup range, both operator estimates.

checklist.task: Choose your primary office location
checklist.instructions: The annual fee is $500 per primary location, so one office keeps costs down. Zoning and siting rules for HCSF offices were not found. Check local zoning for your chosen address. Office rent is an operator estimate of $1,200–$5,500/month by size; no NJ commercial rent benchmark was retrieved. Do not use HUD residential FMRs as an office rent proxy.

checklist.task: Create your account on the NJ Regulated Business Licensure Portal
checklist.instructions: HCSF applicants file online at https://rgbportal.dca.njoag.gov/. Register an account with the owner's email so you control access and renewal notices. Cost: $0. Time: same day.

checklist.task: Submit the online initial registration with the $500 application fee
checklist.instructions: Complete the online application for initial registration and pay the $500 application fee at filing. Upload the practitioner supervisor's licence, insurance certificate, bond (or waiver proof) and the certifications. Save the confirmation and keep a full PDF copy.

checklist.task: Plan for 30–60 days of processing
checklist.instructions: DCA processes applications within 30 to 60 days on average. That is a reported average, not a rule-stated deadline. Do not start marketing as a registered firm or placing aides until registration is issued. Use the wait to hire the office team and prepare the policies.

checklist.task: Do not operate before registration is issued
checklist.instructions: No penalty amount is claimed in this research. A $500-per-day figure appears in 2020 legislation, and its enactment was not verified. Treat unregistered operation as a serious violation and wait for the registration confirmation.

checklist.task: Check how P.L. 2026, c.45 affects your first registration and renewal date
checklist.instructions: P.L. 2026, c.45 (signed July 22, 2026) moved the annual registration expiration from June 30 to September 30. Registrations that had already renewed for 2026-2027 are automatically extended to Sept. 30, 2027. The Sept. 30, 2026 date has passed. Call DCA to confirm the exact expiration and renewal steps for a registration issued now. The act's text was not retrieved.

checklist.task: Calendar the 30-day change-reporting rule
checklist.instructions: Report written changes to information in your application to DCA within 30 calendar days of the change (officers, owners, location, supervisor and so on). Assign one person to own this task.

checklist.task: Apply to your accrediting body early
checklist.instructions: Accreditation must be obtained within 12 months of initial registration and evidence of accreditation is required at each renewal (from May 21, 2019). Start the accreditation application right after registration so the survey happens with real client files. Cost: operator estimate $3,000–$10,000; get quotes.

checklist.task: Write the policies and procedures manual
checklist.instructions: Cover intake, care plans, RN supervision and delegation records, aide screening, EVV, complaints, infection control, emergency plans, abuse reporting and records. Match the accreditor's standards. Budget $1,500–$6,000 (operator estimate) or build from accreditor templates reviewed by counsel.

checklist.task: Create delegation and supervision documentation templates
checklist.instructions: The supervising practitioner must document in the patient's record every task delegated to a homemaker-home health aide. Build a care plan and delegation form so every task is listed and signed before service starts.

checklist.task: Prepare a loss-of-accreditation response procedure
checklist.instructions: Any loss of accreditation must be reported to the Division within 10 days. Add this to your compliance calendar and name a responsible person.

checklist.task: Draft client service agreements
checklist.instructions: State the hourly rate, minimum visit length, cancellation terms, services included and excluded, billing terms and complaint process. Have the attorney review. Keep the model's $38/hour private-pay benchmark in mind, but price from your local competitors.

checklist.task: Confirm there is no HCSF staffing-ratio or inspection rule you are missing
checklist.instructions: Staffing ratios, administrator qualifications and training hours, inspection or survey frequency and capacity limits were not found in primary text for HCSFs. Ask DCA directly and ask your accreditor what its standards require. Document the answers.

checklist.task: Hire only actively certified, agency-employed homemaker-home health aides
checklist.instructions: An HCSF may place only actively certified homemaker-home health aides who are employed by the agency. Verify each aide's certificate on the Board of Nursing lookup before the first shift and again at each renewal. Do not use independent-contractor aides.

checklist.task: Understand that a CHHA may not work privately
checklist.instructions: A certified homemaker-home health aide may not work privately under NJ rules. Place aides only through the agency and do not allow side arrangements with clients. Include this in the aide handbook and employment agreement.

checklist.task: Know the CHHA certification route for recruits
checklist.instructions: Training must be at least 76 hours (60 classroom plus 16 clinical) in a Board-approved program. The Board will not issue the certificate until a criminal history check clears the applicant. Applicants can call the Board of Nursing Call Center at 973-504-6430 (Mon–Fri 8:30 a.m.–4:30 p.m.). Verify the current training rules at N.J.A.C. 13:37-14; the training book was revised 6/13/2019.

checklist.task: Budget for aide certification fees if you reimburse recruits
checklist.instructions: The Board application fee is $50 (nonrefundable) per application. A Board reactivation form cites a $30 biennial renewal fee, but that form is undated, so confirm both amounts on current Board pages. Reimbursement is optional; the model carries $0–$500 at startup.

checklist.task: Track CHHA certificate expirations (every two years)
checklist.instructions: Certificates expire every two years. Keep a roster with each aide's certificate number and expiry. Remove from the schedule any aide whose certificate has lapsed. Inactive certificates need reactivation through the Board.

checklist.task: Recruit aides at a wage that works for the market
checklist.instructions: The model uses $17.83/hour, which is the NJ median for home health and personal care aides (O*NET/BLS OEWS May 2025: $37,090 per year). The 25th percentile is $34,680 and the 75th is $44,580. National median is $35,800. Paying below the median risks recruiting, and the aide cost of about $17.83 × 83.2 hours is the largest cost line.

checklist.task: Verify wages against the NJ minimum wage and any local ordinance
checklist.instructions: The state minimum wage in 2026 is $15.92/hour for most employers, and $15.23 for employers with fewer than 6 employees under the small-employer schedule. Local minimum wages in Newark, Jersey City, Paterson and Trenton were not retrieved. Check municipal ordinances if you hire in those cities.

checklist.task: Hire an administrator and set the role
checklist.instructions: No NJ HCSF administrator qualification rule or training requirement was found. Choose someone with home care and compliance experience. The model uses an operator-estimate salary of $60,000 (20 clients), $75,000 (40) and $80,000 (60). Verify locally.

checklist.task: Hire a scheduler / intake and billing coordinator
checklist.instructions: The model uses 0.5 FTE for 20 clients, 1 FTE for 40 and 2 FTE for 60 clients. The wage proxy is the NJ 75th-percentile aide wage ($44,580), because NJ office-staff wages were not retrieved. Staffing levels are operator estimates.

checklist.task: Screen every hire
checklist.instructions: Run reference checks and background checks before the first client visit. CHHA certification already requires a Board criminal history check, but run your own checks for non-certified office staff. Keep the files for accreditation. Budget is within recruiting and onboarding costs ($25 per client-month, operator estimate).
checklist.cite: Agency policy; Board of Nursing criminal history check

checklist.task: Register as an NJ employer for unemployment, disability and WF/SWF contributions
checklist.instructions: Register through NJDOL Employer Services. The 2026 taxable wage base for UI and WF/SWF is $44,800. The new-employer rate for July 2025–June 2026 was 2.6825% UI plus 0.1175% WF/SWF (2.80%), and the employer disability rate for new employers was 0.50%. The July 2026–June 2027 rate was not verified, so confirm it at registration.

checklist.task: Buy workers' compensation before the first employee starts
checklist.instructions: NJ requires workers' compensation from the first employee. Operating uninsured is a disorderly persons offense (up to $5,000 per 10-day period, per a secondary guide). Sole proprietors, partners and LLC members can elect in. The class-code manual rate was not retrieved; the model uses a 7% payroll load as an operator estimate. NJ approved a 4.3% overall rate-level decrease effective 1/1/2026. Get broker quotes.
checklist.cite: NJ workers' compensation requirement; CRIB Circular 2510

checklist.task: Set up a payroll service
checklist.instructions: Use a provider that handles federal, NJ UI/WF/SWF/TDI/FLI and sick leave. The model's burden is 11.55% payroll tax plus 7% workers' comp plus 4% benefits (partly operator estimates). Have the payroll provider confirm actual rates. Time: 1 week.

checklist.task: Classify caregivers correctly and pay for travel and overtime
checklist.instructions: The model adds 4% paid non-billable time (travel, orientation) as an operator estimate. Confirm wage-and-hour treatment of travel time and live-in or overnight shifts with counsel. Track hours through EVV or timekeeping.
checklist.cite: NJ wage and hour law (confirm with counsel)

checklist.task: Add employer paid-sick-leave and benefit policies
checklist.instructions: The model carries 4% benefits including paid sick leave as an operator estimate. Write the policy in the employee handbook. Confirm the current NJ requirements with your payroll provider or attorney.

checklist.task: Select scheduling, billing and EVV-capable software
checklist.instructions: Pick software that captures visit start and stop, supports private-pay invoicing and can interface with the state EVV aggregator. The model assumes $250–$800/month base plus $12 per client (operator estimates). Get vendor quotes and demos. Whether providers pay EVV or aggregator fees was not found.

checklist.task: Understand NJ EVV rules before any Medicaid billing
checklist.instructions: The Cures Act requires EVV for Medicaid personal care and home health services in the home. NJ lists mobile apps, landline phones and FOB devices as EVV tools. A plan bulletin states personal care services must use EVV since January 1, 2021 and home health since January 1, 2023. HHAeXchange is the NJ aggregator. Self-directed services are covered except live-in caregivers.

checklist.task: Decide whether to enroll with NJ FamilyCare / MCOs (optional, not required for private pay)
checklist.instructions: On verified rates the Medicaid-only models lose money (100 clients: -$11,307/month; 200 clients: -$11,037/month) and the 50/50 mixed model is about break-even. MCO-contracted rates are not public. Only pursue Medicaid after you obtain written contracted rates from MCOs and rerun the model. The CY2026 provider enrollment steps and fees were not verified (a secondary source cites $730). Confirm with DMAHS/NJMMIS.

checklist.task: Learn how NJ Medicaid personal care money flows
checklist.instructions: MLTSS operates through five managed care plans (Aetna Better Health of NJ, Fidelis Care, Horizon NJ Health, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan of NJ, Wellpoint, per a secondary source). The state contracts with MCOs rather than paying per service. The FFS state plan rate for PCA (T1019, 15-minute unit) is $26.68/hour effective July 1, 2024. Horizon's 2023 notice listed a state-mandated minimum of $25.16/hour, so MCO rates may differ.

checklist.task: Learn the Medicaid PCA authorization rules
checklist.instructions: A physician or practitioner must certify medical necessity in writing to the HCSF at initial application and annually. PCA is not authorized when the purpose is companionship, respite or stand-alone supervision. A secondary source reports a 40-hour weekly cap under N.J.A.C. 10:60-3.8(g); the cap text was not retrieved, so verify it.

checklist.task: Know the Personal Preference Program (PPP) and its implications
checklist.instructions: PPP is a self-directed option where the participant hires their own PCAs. The budget is authorized PCA hours times the current rate. Self-directed PCA is paid under the 1915(j) methodology. A secondary source says fiscal intermediaries (Palco or PPL) are assigned by MCO, and that no PPP rate card is published. PPP competes with agency PCA, so understand it as a referral-source and competitor consideration.

checklist.task: Check MLTSS eligibility basics so you can screen referrals
checklist.instructions: Adults 21+ must need hands-on help with three or more ADLs (or supervision and cueing if cognitively impaired). Applicants must be 65+ or under 65 and blind or disabled. Screening is through the county Area Agency on Aging / ADRC. Secondary sources give the 2026 single-applicant limits as $2,982 income and $2,000 assets; verify before telling a family.

checklist.task: Build a cash-flow plan for Medicaid claims lag
checklist.instructions: Medicaid payment timing and EVV claim denials were not verified for NJ. Model at least 30–60 days of receivables for any Medicaid census as a planning assumption, and keep payroll reserves. The mixed model needs about $296,695 in cash, and the 100-client Medicaid model about $627,408, per the pro forma.

checklist.task: Set your private-pay price against local competitors
checklist.instructions: CareScout 2025 puts the NJ median for a non-medical in-home caregiver at $38/hour ($86,944/year at 44 hours/week). The national median is $35/hour. The 2024 Genworth survey listed NJ home health aide at $7,055/month. This is a statewide median, not an agency price, and metros differ. Call several local agencies for their rates. Do not price at $38 without that check.

checklist.task: Build referral relationships
checklist.instructions: Contact hospital discharge planners, rehab facilities, senior living communities, elder-law attorneys, geriatric care managers and county ADRCs. No official referral-source or market-share data was found, so track your own referral sources from day one. Budget is $1,500–$3,500/month (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Size demand in your target counties
checklist.instructions: June 2026 NJ FamilyCare enrollment was 1,799,053, including 305,168 aged, blind and disabled members (107,921 aged; 196,382 disabled) and 65,102 people in home and community-based waiver programs. Essex County had 37,894 ABD members. These show Medicaid demand but not private-pay demand. NJ 65+ population data was not gathered.

checklist.task: Launch a website and local search presence
checklist.instructions: List your registration status accurately, your accreditation once you have it, your service area and your intake phone line. Budget $2,000–$10,000 (operator estimate). Do not claim accreditation before you hold it.

checklist.task: Consider the competitive alternatives you will face
checklist.instructions: PACE became available in all 21 NJ counties in January 2026 (secondary source). PPP and JACC are other state options; JACC may be budget capped. Know how clients may choose among these so you can explain your private-pay value.

checklist.task: Capitalize for the ramp-up deficit
checklist.instructions: Modeled cash needed before reaching profit: about $69,020 for the 20-client agency, $116,006 for 40 clients and $188,309 for 60 clients, with first profit months 8, 9 and 10. These come from the pro forma ramp assumptions (operator estimates). Raise this amount before you start hiring.

checklist.task: Track census against break-even
checklist.instructions: At default settings the 40-client private-pay agency breaks even near 54.6% occupancy (about 22 clients), the 60-client near 55.2% and the 20-client near 70.4%. Review weekly census, hours per client, aide cost per hour and billed rate. Replace the model's operator estimates with your actuals after 90 days.

checklist.task: Stress test hours per client and wage
checklist.instructions: The 80 billable hours per client-month and 4% non-billable time are operator estimates. Rerun the model with fewer hours (for example 60) and with a higher wage to see the margin. Keep the aide wage at or above the $15.92 minimum, and check the metro minimum wage.

checklist.task: Set up client invoicing and payment processing
checklist.instructions: The model assumes 1.5% blended processing on private-pay invoices (operator estimate). Offer ACH to lower costs. Send invoices weekly or biweekly and set collection terms in the service agreement.

checklist.task: Renew HCSF registration on time
checklist.instructions: The annual fee is $500 per primary location. Renewal requires evidence of accreditation. The expiration date is now September 30 (moved from June 30). Calendar the renewal 60 days ahead. The renewal fee schedule under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-7.1 and the text of 13.5 were not retrieved, so confirm the current fee and steps on the portal.

checklist.task: File the annual financial statement
checklist.instructions: HCSFs must still submit the annual financial statement even though the audit and enhanced financial reporting requirements under N.J.A.C. 13:45B-13.5A(b)-(e) are reported suspended. The rule text says by July 1 each year for the preceding calendar year. That conflicts with the Sept. 30 registration date reported by the law firm. Confirm the due date with DCA and ask your CPA to prepare it.

checklist.task: Monitor DCA guidance on implementing P.L. 2026, c.45
checklist.instructions: HCSFs are advised to monitor Division guidance on implementation. Subscribe to DCA notices and review your CPA's and attorney's updates. Rule revisions replacing the suspended audit provisions had not been located.

checklist.task: Keep insurance and bond current
checklist.instructions: Renew the $1,000,000 GPL policy, workers' compensation, auto and the $10,000 bond (unless waived) on schedule. Send updated certificates to DCA when they change, within the 30-day change window where it applies.

checklist.task: Audit RN supervision and delegation files quarterly
checklist.instructions: Spot check that every client record shows tasks delegated to aides and documented by the supervising practitioner, that only actively certified aides are scheduled, and that Medicaid clients have a current practitioner certification of need.

checklist.task: Update the NJ UI/WF/SWF rates each July
checklist.instructions: The July 2026–June 2027 new-employer rate was not verified. Check the NJDOL rate notice each year and update payroll and the model.

checklist.task: Monitor federal Medicaid changes that may affect Medicaid demand
checklist.instructions: NJ DHS says more than 540,000 expansion adults would be subject to community engagement requirements, with work requirements for certain ABP adults 19–64 beginning Jan. 1, 2027 per one DMAHS page (another page says Fall 2026). Most affected members would renew every 6 months. The effect on personal care demand was not quantified. Watch for changes if you serve Medicaid clients.

checklist.task: Re-verify every figure before you rely on it
checklist.instructions: Many facts here came from search-result excerpts of the cited pages, and several are secondary sources. Before you spend, re-check the HCSF fee, bond, insurance, accreditation and registration-date details against the live DCA pages, and call DCA at (973) 504-6367 (from an older guide; verify the number).

checklist.task: Review and re-price annually
checklist.instructions: NJ hourly home care prices have risen roughly 89% to 93% since 2014 per a secondary report, and CareScout releases new figures each year. Compare your rates and aide wages to the newest CareScout and BLS releases and adjust the model.
